  "a.": "Each sentence consists of a subject noun followed by a verb containing the object’s root: SUBJECT + PREFIX–OBJECT–VERB ENDING.

Roots: pę ‘deer’, hų ‘cedar’, t'oy ‘person’, ki ‘blanket’, p'ǫy ‘brother’, ci ‘eye’, ka ‘mother’, p'įw ‘sparrow’, p'i ‘head’.

Verb endings: -mų ‘saw’, -xi ‘waited for’, -mąt'ę ‘hit’.

Subject nouns have two number patterns:
• People and animals: -na singular, -nemą plural.
• Other things: -nemą singular, -ne plural.
Thus -nemą indicates opposite numbers in the two classes.

Possessive prefixes are ki- ‘our’, ką- ‘your’, i- ‘their’, and ą- ‘his’. These take an additional m before nouns ending in -nemą and w before nouns ending in -ne; neither is added with -na.

The verb prefix reflects both subject number and object number/class. The examples establish:
• Singular subject + singular person/animal object: no prefix.
• Plural subject + singular person/animal object: i-.
• Singular subject + plural person/animal object or singular thing object: i-.
• Plural subject + plural person/animal object or singular thing object: ipi-.
• Plural subject + plural thing object: iw-.

For example, imt'oynemą is i-m-t'oy-nemą ‘their people’, and iwhųmų is iw-hų-mų ‘saw the cedars’, giving ‘Their people saw the cedars.’"
}
